scenes.visual: Title card: Cutting the Bridge.

scenes.tts: A key flashes on a screen. The man says he saw nothing. Yet his left hand picks out the key. How?
scenes.visual: A man fixates a dot. A key appears briefly left of the dot. Behind a screen his left hand lifts a key from a tray. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: A key flashes on a screen. The man says he saw nothing. Yet his left hand picks out the key. How?

scenes.tts: Cutting the forebrain commissures was used to treat epilepsy that drugs could not control. The corpus callosum is the largest commissure.
scenes.visual: A brain seen from the midline. The corpus callosum is highlighted, then a cut line appears through it.
scenes.narration: Cutting the forebrain commissures was used to treat epilepsy that drugs could not control. The corpus callosum is the largest commissure.

scenes.tts: In nineteen sixty-two, Gazzaniga, Bogen and Sperry reported one such patient, W J.
scenes.caption: In 1962, Gazzaniga, Bogen and Sperry reported one such patient, W.J.
scenes.visual: Title text: Gazzaniga, Bogen and Sperry, 1962. Patient W.J.
scenes.narration: In 1962, Gazzaniga, Bogen and Sperry reported one such patient, W.J.

scenes.tts: Blindfolded, he could use familiar objects with his left hand. But he could not name them.
scenes.visual: A blindfolded man uses a comb with his left hand. A speech bubble stays empty.
scenes.narration: Blindfolded, he could use familiar objects with his left hand. But he could not name them.

scenes.tts: First, the crossings. At the optic chiasm, only the fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross.
scenes.visual: Both eyes and the optic paths seen from above. Nasal fibres from each retina cross at the chiasm; temporal fibres stay on their own side.
scenes.narration: First, the crossings. At the optic chiasm, only the fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross.

scenes.tts: So everything left of the point he stares at reaches the right hemisphere, from both eyes. The hemifield matters, not the eye.
scenes.visual: The left half of the visual scene is tinted. Its signals from both eyes run to the right hemisphere. Label: hemifield, not eye.
scenes.narration: So everything left of the point he stares at reaches the right hemisphere, from both eyes. The hemifield matters, not the eye.

scenes.tts: A brief flash reduces the chance that he looks toward it. We still monitor his gaze and discard trials with an eye movement, which could expose the picture to the other hemisphere.
scenes.visual: A brief flash on the left. On screen only: brief flash, e.g. 150 ms or less; maintain fixation, track gaze and reject eye-movement trials.
scenes.narration: A brief flash reduces the chance that he looks toward it. We still monitor his gaze and discard trials with an eye movement, which could expose the picture to the other hemisphere.

scenes.tts: Touch from the left hand reaches the right hemisphere. And each hand is controlled mainly by the opposite hemisphere.
scenes.visual: Touch path from the left hand ascends and crosses in the medulla to the right hemisphere. A motor path from the right hemisphere descends to the left hand.
scenes.narration: Touch from the left hand reaches the right hemisphere. And each hand is controlled mainly by the opposite hemisphere.

scenes.tts: Now apply the rule. You can say only what reaches the speaking hemisphere. In most people, that is the left.
scenes.visual: Rule card from chapter one. The left hemisphere is labelled: speaks.
scenes.narration: Now apply the rule. You can say only what reaches the speaking hemisphere. In most people, that is the left.

scenes.tts: The key in the left field reaches only the right hemisphere. With the bridge cut, it has no route to speech.
scenes.visual: The key signal lights the right hemisphere and stops at the cut callosum.
scenes.narration: The key in the left field reaches only the right hemisphere. With the bridge cut, it has no route to speech.

scenes.tts: So he cannot name it, and says he saw nothing. But his right hemisphere feels with and controls the left hand, which finds the key.
scenes.visual: A speech bubble: I saw nothing. The left hand, lit in the same colour as the right hemisphere, picks out the key.
scenes.narration: So he cannot name it, and says he saw nothing. But his right hemisphere feels with and controls the left hand, which finds the key.

scenes.tts: Now his eyes are closed, and a spoon is placed in his right hand. Can he name it?
scenes.visual: Eyes closed. A spoon in the right hand behind the screen. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: Now his eyes are closed, and a spoon is placed in his right hand. Can he name it?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: Yes. Touch from the right hand crosses in the medulla to the left hemisphere, which usually speaks.
scenes.visual: The touch path from the right hand crosses to the left hemisphere. A speech bubble: spoon.
scenes.narration: Yes. Touch from the right hand crosses in the medulla to the left hemisphere, which usually speaks.

scenes.tts: If speech were on the right, the naming answers would flip. The hands would still follow the same crossings.
scenes.visual: The speaks label slides to the right hemisphere. Only the speech bubbles swap: the left-field key is now named, the spoon is not. The hand results stay where they were.
scenes.narration: If speech were on the right, the naming answers would flip. The hands would still follow the same crossings.

scenes.tts: Still, the disconnected right hemisphere understands some spoken words. It is mute more often than it is deaf.
scenes.visual: The right hemisphere glows faintly along its ventral road. Label: understands some words, cannot say them.
scenes.narration: Still, the disconnected right hemisphere understands some spoken words. It is mute more often than it is deaf.

scenes.tts: That fits the route. Understanding words gets help from both sides, but the road to speech usually runs on the left.
scenes.visual: The route map from chapter one: ventral road on both sides, dorsal road and planner on the left.
scenes.narration: That fits the route. Understanding words gets help from both sides, but the road to speech usually runs on the left.

scenes.tts: The tidy rule has exceptions in two later patients. That debate is in the lesson.
scenes.visual: A small card: exceptions, two patients, 2017; see Going deeper.
scenes.narration: The tidy rule has exceptions in two later patients. That debate is in the lesson.

scenes.tts: His right hemisphere can still see, feel and understand some words. But he cannot say what never reaches the speaking hemisphere.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: you can say only what reaches the speaking hemisphere.
scenes.narration: His right hemisphere can still see, feel and understand some words. But he cannot say what never reaches the speaking hemisphere.
